utterances.text: No. That is against the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the Crisis Staff pass a decision dismissing the chief of SUP?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think that I have already said that anybody within the ranks of the police was appointed and dismissed by the minister, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we are on that subject, could you explain to us briefly the relationship between the Municipal Assembly - this is something that we know from the constitution and the legal system - and the police station within a certain municipality. Who gives the orders and on the basis of which instructions --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. Firstly, it isn't in the summary; and secondly, the question which has just been asked is: Who gives the orders within a certain municipality. That is an entirely theoretical question. We're concerned here with a factual situation which occurred in a certain municipality in the indictment period. The question my learned friend is asking the witness can only relate, if the witness knows, to that municipality, because that's what we're concerned with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, in my summary, item 2, formation of Serb police forces, including the internal organisation and relation towards the other authorities. So I don't see any particular reason not to have some additional facts on that issue from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that there can be a comparison with Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With Samac municipality. And I will directly ask him about the Doboj region and Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, as long as it's very, very restricted, so that we get details on the municipality we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please explain to us specifically now, first of all in relation to the regional centre of security in Doboj and then the public security station in Samac, how do they actually operate? And the municipality, that is to say, the social political community in Samac. Could they do anything, and were they involved in the hierarchy that pertained to the terms of reference of the police? Can you explain this to us on the example of Samac and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. Could both speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters are complaining. Please do slow down, both of you. I just want to emphasise that the question is related to the period in the indictment, the operations then, not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have heard the Presiding Judge, Her Honour Judge Mumba. So we are interested in that period from when the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska was established, the beginning of 1992, as you said, and we are interested in the period of the indictment, that is to say from the end of 1993, and we are speaking about that period.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to the Presiding Judge for speaking so fast. I will try to be briefer and slower.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: At that time the municipality authorities could ask the public security station to do some things. For example, to regulate the traffic within the area, to reinforce the control of public law and order in a certain area, et cetera. After that, the chief of the public security station would have to ask for the consent and approval of the head of the centre for regional centre for security. So there was no hierarchy. The municipal organs could turn to the public security station for help and the head of the public security station would ask for approval or consent for having something done or not done. That is the way it operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, in terms of certain pre-investigative procedures in the proceedings against certain persons, what was the role of the police there, and what did the police station, the public security station, as the lowest level within this organisation, carry out this procedure? How did they carry out their cooperation and how did they relate to higher authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Within the field of crime investigation, they had the right and duty to bring criminal charges. They did whatever the police does anywhere in the world, that is to say that they gathered evidence, written materials, witness statements, et cetera, and then they reported to the centre about that if serious crimes were involved. If lesser crimes were involved, they directly submitted charge sheets to the municipal public prosecutor. I don't know whether you are interested in this, but at that time there were distinctions in terms of the crimes involved. So in Republika Srpska, we had the basic courts and the district courts. The basic courts dealt with lesser crimes and district courts dealt with more serious crimes, those that involved sentences of five years onwards. So it is the public security station that submitted charge sheets to the basic court, and it was the centre -- the regional centre for security that provided these charge sheets to the district courts. So the district court and the regional centre of public security had jurisdictions that coincided. That is how these powers were divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just bear for a second with me. I have to check the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We were just waiting for a legal expression to come up, because that was complicated, and we're also waiting for the transcript to be finished on the computer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that this rate of speaking is too fast for the court reporters and for the interpreters. Could the speakers kindly slow down for the record as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Slavko, you understand that you have to slow down so that the record is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction. When you said that charge sheets, are they submitted to the Court or to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: To the basic prosecutor, the municipal prosecutor, and to the district prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question pertains to a relationship during the war conflict, namely, between the police force and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The recording on the monitor seems to have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can start and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my previous question was whether you had any personal knowledge whether you could tell us something about the relationship during the war, during the state of war, the state of war conflicts between the police force and the military. Of course, we're interested in the period from April 1992 until the end of December 1993, in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I think we have a problem with the transcript, with LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has been informed that the problem requires some time to rectify, so I'm afraid we'll have to adjourn now and continue in the afternoon, at 1430 hours. Hopefully during the lunch break the problem will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes we'll continue our proceedings. We've been informed that the technical problem has been sorted out. So we'll sit for one and a half hours and take ten minutes' break and continue after 1700 hours. We are sitting under Rule 15 bis because Judge Lindholm has had to go away. Please continue, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paleksic, before the break we had a problem with the transcript. I'm going to repeat my question. So we're talking about the period from April 1992 until December 1993. Can you tell us what you yourself know about the relations between the police and the military during the war. What do you know about this relationship?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the police worked on the basis of the law of the interior and the relevant by-laws. It had its own powers. The army worked according to the law on the army, and they had their own powers. However, these powers became intertwined if there were joint actions in the territory where the police was engaged as well. Then the police forces would be resubordinated to the military command, to put it in military terms. So, for example, in the territory that was held by a particular corps, a police company would take orders from the military commander of that area. Those were the only joint activities of the military and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me: In terms of procedure, if in that situation a crime were to be committed in times of war, and since there were both police and military forces in the area, could you tell us who was in charge of taking action in terms of the pre-trial and criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: For the military, it was the military organs that were there charge, and for civilians, the civilian organs, that is to say, the office of the prosecutor and the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you personally have any knowledge about the alleged crime that was committed in the month of May in Crkvina by the members of paramilitary units in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I learned of this case only when I was legal assistant in these proceedings. In 1992, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, and if you did, when did you find out about certain crimes that were committed by Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I learned about them during these proceedings as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it that you learned about what Stevan Todorovic had done? Do you know whether he was convicted? Did he admit to something, or what do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I only know what I read in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While your commission, and you personally, were in Samac, did Stevan Todorovic speak about any crimes perhaps, or those committed by him as well as other persons in the territory of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the atmosphere in Samac in 1992, December 1992, in relation to the fact whether there were or were not any refugees among the civilian population, and what were your observations during the work of your commission? What did you personally observe while you were in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: It was obvious, and we also found out as we talked to people and employees of the police that there were a lot of refugees, especially from the area of Posavina, that is to say Brod, Odzak, Derventa, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you assess the numbers involved in 1992 in Samac, December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think it was thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. The summaries which Your Honour has ordered my learned friend to provide as to facts about this -- about which this witness would give evidence say nothing about refugees or an estimation of refugee numbers or anything about the refugee situation. The closest it gets is political and military aspects, but I can't see how refugee comes into that. The witness is described as the former chief of the legal department of the regional police centre at Doboj. He's here to talk about Stevan Todorovic, as far as the summary says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, my learned friend can turn to page 7 on the summary and then he can find the other factual allegations, including the number of citizens in Odzak and Samac municipality, as well as the first paragraph in the summary, the general situation in Posavina regarding political and military aspects. And finally, this witness might be an eyewitness of the period in December 1992 in Samac with regard to that issue, nothing more. [Trial Chamber confers] .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that the question can be asked. It will be allowed, because it does concern some of the political aspects of the movements of the people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paleksic, just tell me about what you saw yourself and what you found out, both in your conversations with persons in Samac regarding this subject that we mentioned, that is, refugees. So the number and also the atmosphere that prevailed in Samac in general. Could you tell us what you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since I lived in Doboj at the time, I know that many people in the places that I mentioned moved or fled to Doboj, Samac, Petrovo, Teslic, and so on, and I know that we talked about that, because this was an inevitable subject anywhere, and I saw such persons myself while I spent those three or four days in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic, but before you move on, I'd just like to go back to the question and answer on page 50, where your question was concerning legal procedure in times of war, and that's line 7 on page 50. And the witness's answer on line 13, he says: For the military, it was the military organs that were in charge; for civilians, the civilian organs, that is to say, the office of the prosecutor and the court. Mr. Paleksic, I wonder whether you know what the procedure would have been if a person in Bosanski Samac had been arrested during the period after April 17th, 1992 for having a weapon without a licence. So if we had a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosnian Croat arrested in Bosanski Samac on or after April 17th, 1992 for having a gun or other weapon without a licence, would that person have been amenable to the civilian courts, the office of the prosecutor, the civilian courts, and all of the fundamental human rights and guarantees under international law that that person is entitled to, including right to a speedy trial, right to counsel, right to be presumed innocent, and so on and so forth, if you know, as a person with your legal background and involvement in these issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very complex question. I think that in all towns there were lists of military conscripts, and if this had to do with a military conscript - now I'm telling you about what I think - then it is the military prosecutor's office that would receive the charge sheet. I think that that was the practice that prevailed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. If the person was not a military conscript, if the person was a citizen of Bosanski Samac who had not been conscripted as such, if you don't know, obviously say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was done at that time. I don't know what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paleksic, in that period -- actually, as concerns your personal knowledge regarding the period from April 1992 to December 1993, was the civilian judiciary operating in the area, in Doboj, where the regional security centre was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The regional judiciary was functioning. I'm not sure about Samac, but I think Samac actually never had a court of its own or a prosecutor's office. As far as I know, they only had an office from a court of law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But where was the seat of that court of law?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: In Doboj or in Modrica. Please don't take my word for it. At that time I was not involved in judicial matters, either in Doboj or in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me: If a crime would be committed by a member of a paramilitary unit, which judicial organ would be in charge of such a person? Perhaps I should ask you before that whether you know who the volunteers were subordinated to. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I presume that they were subordinated to the military. I was not in the military, but that's my assumption, according to the very logic of these matters, it would have to be the military organs that would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. I object to this sort of evidence. My learned friend should know the answer to the questions he's putting to the witness, and if it's going to be "I presume," it shouldn't be asked in the first place. That evidence is of no value to the Trial Chamber if the witness can't answer it. He should not be asked these questions in the first place, which don't appear to be in the summary anyway. There's nothing there about paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. This time the Prosecution's objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Paleksic, what do you know yourself about the relationship between Stevan Todorovic and Blagoje Simic in the period from April 1992 until the end of 1993? How could you describe that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I felt that the relations were such that they always bordered on some kind of a quarrel. In terms of what I knew towards the end of 1993, these were two quite different persons. Their characters were quite different. Mr. Simic was a rather quiet, responsible person, whereas Mr. Todorovic was, well, prone to arbitrary behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a bit more detail? What kind of arbitrary behaviour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I already said that Mr. Todorovic did not respect authority. The institutional way of work. He did quite a few things on his own. That is what I know in terms of -- from the relationship between the regional security centre and the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the regional centre in Doboj, were there certain comments or complaints regarding this kind of behaviour of Todorovic, who, after all, was a member of the same service?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: There were, but at that time I was not in charge of resolving such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In relation to the subject that we touched upon a while ago, that is to say, your personal views and also the situation regarding refugees in Samac when you were there, what are your observations regarding the atmosphere that prevailed in Samac, in terms of that number of refugees? Because, of course, we are talking about December 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know any details, but I know that in all towns where there was a large number of refugees, there were problems between the local population and the refugees, because it was impossible to accommodate everyone because of the frustration of the people who had fled because they had lost their property. Some of them had lost their nearest and dearest as well. So it was hard to establish this kind of contact. Actually, I'm talking about Doboj more than I'm talking about Samac, because I spent only a short time in Samac, so I could not observe the situation in its entirety, but it was the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the number of crimes committed and the security atmosphere, safety and security atmosphere that prevailed, what are your observations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The number of crimes was on the rise, especially those pertaining to property, namely, robberies, lootings, as far as I know, murders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished my examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You want me to go first, Your Honour, or the other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes. Any other questions from Defence counsel. I see none.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paleksic, have I pronounced it correctly? Paleksic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position in 1992 at the Doboj regional centre, I think you said you were the chief of legal and personnel. Have I got that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that also -- sorry. In that position you had access to all the personnel files of all the police officers under the Doboj regional command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, in 1992, or rather, in August and October 1992, no, but after that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, of course, included the police chief of Bosanski Samac, or Samac, as it then was, Mr. Stevan Todorovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position, did it also involve responsibility for investigating complaints against police officers under the general command or within the responsibility of the Doboj regional centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. If I can explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The department for personnel and legal affairs carried out administrative tasks in the public security centre, and also for all public security stations. Decisions and -- it issued decisions and identification, and the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence of the witness. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness repeat the answer, especially the last part. The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got up to, "it issued decisions and identification and the" -- and we didn't get that last bit. Could you tell us what that last bit was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: We carried out only administrative tasks for the centre and for the public security stations, and the monitoring of the work of the public security station was in the jurisdiction of the chief of the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the chief of the public security centre in Doboj, where you worked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Samac in December 1992 for three or four days, you were investigating complaints about the running of the police station, and you had a specific area; is that correct, to investigate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but everybody worked in their own field, so I reviewed, in accordance with the instructions of the minister, the shortcomings that appeared in the issuance of public papers, identification, and also drivers' licences and traffic permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention to the transcript. The answer of Mr. Paleksic, we don't see the personnel issues, and he said clearly that also he was in charge for investigation. But maybe my learned friend can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In charge of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of personnel. Personnel issues in terms of the personnel of the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe he can repeat the answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just clarify that last part. My learned friend Mr. Pantelic said you also referred to personnel issues. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you just said about your responsibility for investigating personnel issues.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Our inspection meant, understood for us whether to review whether all the police officers had appropriate work papers as required under the law in order to work in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went there in December 1992 with was it two or three other people? Just the figure.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I was there with four other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were specifically charged - correct me if I'm wrong - with investigating the running of the police station under the direction of Stevan Todorovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: That was the task of the whole team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you embarked upon your visit to the station in Samac, you of course discussed with the other members of the team how you were going to approach your task, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. The order came from the ministry of the -- for internal affairs, and we went, two of us, Mico Novakovic and myself, and in Vakuf [as interpreted] we met with three other people. I had not seen them before. And when we met, we agreed that upon the division of the overall tasks, each one of us would be monitoring --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- transcript. Page 63, line 1. Here it says Vakuf, and actually, the witness said that they met in Samac. It could make some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we correct that, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met in Samac, the other members of the investigation team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you met there, you agreed upon the division of the task; is that what you're saying, and coordinated how the five of you were going to investigate the running of the Samac police station under Stevan Todorovic's command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Each one of us was responsible for our own field of work. We had a specific task from the minister for internal affairs. I dealt with legal matters, Mr. Saric and Mr. Novakovic dealt with police matters, and Mr. Ostoja Minic dealt with the criminal investigation issues. I think that there was one more member who was monitoring some financial matters, but I can't quite remember who that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you went to Samac, as a person who had access to Stevan Todorovic's personnel file, you looked at his file, didn't you, to find out who you were going to investigate; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: There were no files at that time. There was only a decision issued by the Ministry for Internal Affairs. After that, files were being set up for another year or two. Because many people in the police were -- had the status of refugees, so they didn't have any documents with them. Stations were formed in a rush, so that the administrative part was lagging behind compared to other tasks from the domain of the internal affairs duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your evidence, then, to this Trial Chamber that Stevan Todorovic, as the chief of the Bosanski Samac police station, in December, as of December 1992, did not have a personnel file with the Doboj regional command centre? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim that for sure, but I think that they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the normal course of an investigation, if you're investigating the activities of someone running a police station, you, as a trained investigator, would go to a personnel file to find out what there was against -- what was on the file before you went to the station; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: That is how it should be, but it was war, and many people did not have personnel files. And in the beginning, all the personnel files contained only the letter of appointment or the decision of the appointment. There was no proof of completed education or any other things, so all this was done later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Complaints about -- I withdraw that. How many police stations were under the Doboj central command in December 1992, when you went to Samac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Samac, Brod, Derventa, Doboj, Modrica, Petrovo, and Teslic. Seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence earlier was that the regional command in Doboj received daily reports from the police stations each day on their activities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, not from the regional centres but from the public security stations. When there was a communication established between the centre and the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The regional centre where you worked received -- was receiving, is it correct, daily reports from the Samac public security station in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had access to these daily reports?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I had no access to them. Only the chief of the centre had access.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were specifically charged with investigating matters relating to licensing in Samac. What were the four other people charged with investigating in relation to Stevan Todorovic's activities as head of the police station there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the station had a police department, a criminal investigations department, and a department for personnel and legal affairs. The other members of the team controlled the work of the police, of the inspectors, and the back-up services in the investigations of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What specifically were these four other people investigating in relation to the running of the police station? It's fairly major, you'd agree, for five people to descend from the Ministry of the Interior upon a small police station, each investigating an aspect of it. What was each of them specifically investigating, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The inspectors of the police work were investigating how the police was conducting its duties: Did they act according to regulations, were they trained according to regulations, were they wearing the regulation uniform, and other things as set down in regulations about the work of the police. Those investigating the criminal investigations section were to see how the pre-investigative or pre-criminal procedures were being carried out. Were they being conducted in accordance with the law on -- with criminal law and the law on criminal procedures. So the gathering of evidence, the procedures in taking statements from witnesses, and so on. I was checking the issuance of public documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So none of these five investigators were investigating the murder of someone called Anto Brandic, also known as Antesa, on the 29th of July, 1992, in the Samac police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware of anyone -- these five people investigating the allegation that Todorovic kicked this man to death in the hallway of the police station on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware of any complaint being made about Stevan Todorovic kicking to death Antesa on the 29th of July, 1992, in the police station, under the general command of the Doboj regional police centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, none of these five investigators were investigating an allegation of sexual assault in the Bosanski Samac police station in which Stevan Todorovic beat and kicked a prisoner, Witness A, in the genital area, took him over to another man, who Stevan Todorovic ordered to "bite into his penis." As far as you know, no one was investigating that particular allegation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, none of the five investigators, including yourself, were investigating the -- Todorovic ordering two prisoners, known as C and D, being ordered to perform oral sex on each other in the Samac police station in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The first time I found out about those facts was when I was engaged as a legal assistant on this case. Until then, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, none of the five investigators, including yourself, were investigating the beating of a priest in the Samac police station on the 29th of July, 1992, who was then imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I was only dealing with the issues regarding public documents. Anything else I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, none of the investigators, the five of you, were investigating Todorovic's beating of prisoners in the primary school at Bosanski Samac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know that there were any prisoners in the elementary school at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you're aware, none of you were also investigating Todorovic's participation in the unlawful arrest and detention of non-Serb civilians arrested and detained only because they were non-Serbs, in the Bosanski Samac region?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I must say that I know that I was not investigating that, and I didn't know anything about that. But I cannot say whether any of the other members of the commission investigated it or knew about it. Allow me to respond to the Prosecutor. I don't know about any of these things. Whether others knew about them or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you know, no one of the five of you was investigating the cruel and inhumane treatment of non-Serb civilians in Bosanski Samac, in which Todorovic has admitted his participation in this Trial Chamber, through forced labour assignments, including digging trenches and constructing bunkers on the front line? You weren't investigating that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I did not, but I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know whether the others were investigating -- sorry. I withdraw that. So far as you know, the others weren't investigating the arrest and detention and Todorovic forcing prisoners to sign false statements before December 1992 in the Samac police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you're aware, you don't know whether the other investigators were investigating Todorovic's admitted participation in the deportation of non-Serb civilians only because they were non-Serb, from Samac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: We worked there in the following way: Each one of us worked separately on their tasks and compiled a part of the report, which was then passed on to the ministry. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you know, the others weren't investigating the issuance of orders and directives which violated the rights of non-Serb civilians to equal treatment under the law, infringed upon their enjoyment of basic and fundamental rights, such as an order he signed on the 4th of August, 1992, prohibiting three or more Muslims or Croats from gathering in a public place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Generally, I'm not objecting to the issues that the learned friend from Prosecution would like to explore, but the form of the question is very general and multi-barrelled. First of all, how this witness could know, and he precisely answered on many occasions whether or not the other members of the commission of the team were aware or not about certain events. The proper way of questioning should be what is his personal knowledge of certain events, and then if maybe he heard that the other members of the team were aware, stuff like that. Otherwise it's too general and it's heading nowhere. I tried not to object on these many occasions, but generally I object to this line of questioning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's loaded, Mr. Re. Please split it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm merely putting to the witness, Your Honour, the factual allegations to which Todorovic pleaded guilty and was found guilty of by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That I realise. But it's just that there are too many -- a bit too many issues. Just take them one by one for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As well, I think, Mr. Re, it might be useful to ask the witness directly whether, for example, he and the other members of the commission following their days, through or four days work in the police station, whether they discussed over dinner or a drink or what have you what they had done during the day, and therefore he knew from the other persons directly, you know, what they had found or something similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. I will ask that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think you answered the last question I asked you, and that was in relation to the investigation of orders issued by Mr. Todorovic violating the rights of non-Serb civilians to equal treatment, one of which was an order signed on the 4th of August, 1992, that's four months before you went there with the four others to investigate activities, prohibiting three or four Muslims or Croats from gathering in public places. The question is: Were you or, to your knowledge, any of the other four investigators investigating that specific complaint about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have already said, and I'll try to explain. We received our orders from the ministry -- from the minister of the interior. We did not act on the basis of complaints of citizens or anything like that. I saw that paper only when I started working here at The Hague Tribunal. I did not know about this at all before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the other investigators investigated Todorovic's participation in the plunder and looting of non-Serb property, that's property belonging to Muslims and Croats, in the Samac region?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I said that in Samac I saw for the first time some persons from the Ministry of the Interior, and I did not learn anything about the circumstances that you have referred to just now. The only person I knew on the team was Mico Novakovic, the one who was monitoring the work of the police from the point of view of how well trained they were, whether they were in proper uniform, et cetera. We did not exchange experiences in that situation. Everybody did his own job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to Your Honour's question in a moment, which I'll ask. So is it correct that so far as you're aware, none of the other investigators, so far as you're aware, were investigating any of the specific things which I've just read to you? It's a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any one of them having investigated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as you're aware, as the then chief of legal and personnel in the regional command at Doboj, which was responsible for the oversight of the Samac police station, you weren't aware of any of the complaints of the nature which I've just read to you of murder, torture, ill-treatment, plunder, looting, and so on, against Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I only worked in the domain of personnel and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling the Trial Chamber you heard nothing about Todorovic's activities and his participation in murder, ill-treatment of prisoners, detaining non-Serbs, only because they were non-Serbs, looting and plundering, et cetera, in the period which you worked as -- in the Doboj regional command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Her Honour Judge Williams asked me to ask you in relation to what the other investigators -- the other four people spoke to you about after you had completed your three or four day investigation. What did they tell you about what they had been investigating and what their findings were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: The general assessment was that the situation in the station was not in proper order and that the station was not being managed properly. I did not have any other information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no one mentioned to you there had been a complaint about murder, torture, ill-treatment, detention -- extrajudicial detention on discriminatory grounds only, plundering, looting, sexual assault. None of the other investigators said we've been looking into these terrible allegations about our police station in Samac. The highest it got was things aren't being done properly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: No one said anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already responded, but I wanted to object. I believe that the Prosecutor is being over repetitive. He has already received many answers from this witness and he is now asking him to speculate as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Mr. Lukic's observation is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were an employee of the Ministry of the Interior in 1992 and 1993, were you paid centrally through the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. These resources came from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, the local police chiefs, such as the police chief of Samac in the other stations you mentioned, were they also paid essentially through the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Salaries were sent to the centre for regional security, and the centre then further transferred these funds to public security stations. However, may I just add one thing? It would happen that the entire payroll for the entire regional centre, that is to say, for 1.000 employees, would amount to a certain amount of money that was sufficient for buying a pack of cigarettes only, because there was such rampant inflation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic, as the police chief of Samac, his name, so far as you're concerned, as someone who worked in the Ministry of the Interior, his name would only appear on a Ministry of the Interior payroll, for his job as chief of police; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. He sent reports every day. That's where his name appeared to. He participated in some meetings that were organised by the head of the centre. He signed charge sheets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstand. I'm talking about the payroll, the people who paid him. The only payroll upon which his name should appear as Ministry of the Interior employee and as chief of the Samac police station would be on a Ministry of Interior payroll; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. He appeared on the payroll of the Ministry of the Interior. Whether he appeared on any other payroll is something that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your name, as a serving officer of the Ministry of Interior, appear on any other payrolls other than the Ministry of the Interior's?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mine, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just excuse me for one moment? I think I'm there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about the report you prepared as a result of your three-day visit to Samac. Do you have a copy of that report or the reports the other four investigators prepared in relation to Stevan Todorovic's activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: We all sent our own reports separately. It is forbidden to keep official reports. I believe that this report does exist in the Ministry of the Interior, but I could not have a copy at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can take it from the evidence you've given that you've never heard about the allegations of murder, sexual assault, plundering, looting, all those things I read to you from the sentencing judgement, except when you came into this case, that Dr. Blagoje Simic never mentioned those things to you when he spoke to you, any of those complaints about Stevan Todorovic when he spoke to you at that dinner in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: He did not mention any such thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination? Re-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Paleksic, in principle, you have clarified everything here as regards the questions put by the Prosecutor. Let's just look into a few matters. In relation to what the Prosecutor asked you about salaries, you said that due to truly rampant inflation, this amount was totally devalued, the entire payroll. Tell me: Do you have any personal knowledge as to whether the employees received something else instead of these salaries? Could you please explain this to us? How did things work out? Because people have to live on something.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how were these questions resolved in practice by various institutions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sometimes the Red Cross would give the Ministry of the Interior some basic food supplies, but very rarely. All the rest of us lived on humanitarian aid. I'm sorry that I didn't bring along my membership card. Before the war, I was a person who was well off, but this card shows that for two years I would take a sack of flour, of sugar, some oil, et cetera, every 15 days or every month, and that's the way people lived throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. They couldn't buy a thing using their salaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Paleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Paleksic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are now free. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the next witness is being brought out, can I inform the Court in relation to the joint Defence handwriting expert professor Aleksic, we filed a notice requiring him for examination. The Prosecution no longer requires him for cross-examination and we don't object to tender of his report in the due course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. So the Prosecution notice which was filed is withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear the translation in your headphones? Please, before we commence, please bear in mind, since both you and I speak the same language, we often overlap in our discussion, which necessitates that you take at least a few seconds' pause before you start answering my question and to allow for the interpreters to do their part of the job. Thank you in advance for that. Could you kindly tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ozren Stanimirovic. I'm a medical doctor by profession. I graduated from the medical school in Pristina and I specialised in pulmonology and tuberculosis of the lungs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, will you please tell us when you were born?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th of February, 1948, in Nis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Since when have you been living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Samac on the 18th of April, 1978.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What is your father by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: My father is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your mother?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: My mother is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Are you married? What is your marital status?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I am happily divorced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you married in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and my wife was also a Croat, but we didn't divorce because she was Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this is a personal question, please don't be offended with it, but tell me: When did you divorce?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think that was about two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you have children with your ex-wife?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have one child, and my ex-wife comes to visit her son and her grandchildren, because my son is married and has his own children. We keep seeing each other, but we don't live together any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been living in Samac since 1978. Did you spend the whole time there or was there a period between 1978 and today that you did not live there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of two years in the early 1980s when I went to Belgrade for specialisation, I have lived in Samac all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in addition to your medical specialisation, in your professional career, including the present time, have you completed any other courses of specialised medicine?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not in -- I'm currently doing the specialisation course of family medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that with some medical institution, faculty, or something else?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It is being organised by a Geneva cantonal hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you complete military service?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In 1976 and 1977, the first part of the military service I did in Zrenjanin, and the second part at the military airport in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us how long have you been working? What is your length of service?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: About 25 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current professional position that you hold at the moment?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At the moment I am the head of the pulmonology clinic within the medical centre in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can briefly just lead us through your professional career ever since you started working. Tell us which positions and posts did you hold?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I started as an intern, which is a usual practice and the usual beginnings for every medical doctor. I was a secondary doctor in a chest department in Samac. Then I did my specialisation in this same ward, and eventually I became the head of this ward. For a time, I was also the director of the Samac hospital. During the war, I was a coordinator for the whole of Samac, which means the coordinator for the medical centre in Samac. And for four years I have been the head of the medical clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor: Have you ever been a member of a political party? Were you politically active?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of a few political parties, as an exemplary soldier, I was admitted to the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: While I was in the army. That was a kind of reward, because I was pronounced the best soldier of the battalion. When I left the army and started working, I left this party. When the SDS was in the process of forming, I came to a meeting, so I can be deemed to be one of the founders of the party. So at one point in time when I did not -- started disagreeing with them, I left the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think that was about four or five or even six years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me -- sorry. I interrupted you. You said several parties. Were you a member of any other party in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. I am more or less a kind of decorative member, because I'm not very much interested in politics, and I'm a popular person, and I was one of the doctors who had lived and worked in this municipality for a long time, and people liked to have me around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were one of the founders of the SDS Samac. Can you tell us what year was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a little bit difficult to say now, but I think that was in 1990. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any other persons who were also the founders of the SDS at the time?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, at this meeting there were about some 40 or 50 people. I can't remember all their names. I can remember that in the town of Samac there were very few such people, due to which I automatically became member of the town board. I could not allow myself to be elected by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember, at the time, in the 1990, who was the president, the chairman of the town board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine. His first name was Dusko, but I can't remember his last name. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this period in 1990? Were any other parties established in Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The other parties that were established there, the presidents of those parties were all my friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which parties were established in 1990, whether it was in or around 1990?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, because I was not interested. For example, Sulejman Tihic, the founder of the SDR [as interpreted] in Samac is a friend of mine. The vice-president of the HDZ, I cannot remember his full name. He was a friend of mine, and we knew each other and he was known by the nickname --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter didn't get the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that a certain person was the vice-president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he was a member of the presidency or the vice-presidency. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us your [sic] name for the record.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: His nickname was Pilja, and I don't know his full name. I don't want to be mistaken. We usually call each other in the place where I come from by nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not too sure. I'm a little bit lost with the schedule for today. Is it time for a break now or we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The break will be at 1615.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, 1615. Thank you so much. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Tell me, Dr. Stanimirovic: Apart from the SDA, SDS, and the HDZ, at the local level in Samac, was there -- were there any other parties on the political scene there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was a socialist party, and I attended their first meeting during the war. And the people who lead this party, I know them very well, and we are on good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these, were there any others?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: I forgot to ask you within your personal data whether you are a religious person, and which confession do you belong?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a believer, and I'm an orthodox religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember local elections for the Samac Municipal Assembly? When were they held, and how was the assembly -- or the authority established, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What were your personal observation and knowledge of the situation that prevailed in Samac in the period between the autumn of 1991 and April 1992? How would you characterise this?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There was some indication that the situation will become ugly, but many of my acquaintances did not believe that, that what happened would have happened. We really hoped that it would not come to that. My friends and I were really caught by surprise with all these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe interethnic relations in Samac in that period?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a rather difficult question. I can explain that I used to socialise with people who were my friends, of whom I was fond of, and with whom I still maintain friendly relations. They are all Serbs, Muslims, and Croats equally. So I cannot tell you any specific opinion about interethnic relations in the town itself. I'm not the proper person to give you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard or were you witness to any conflicts along ethnic lines? Were there any explosions? Were there any wounded people? You are a medical doctor, after all. Maybe you had some knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some shootings, although I wasn't on duty. There were some misunderstandings that led to the blockades in the town. But since I knew these people, I felt it was very awkward for me to go and look what was going on, and I preferred to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you knew these people, who are you referring to? I presume you are referring to the people who took part in these blockades or some other people. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 30.000 inhabitants of Samac, I think that about 20.000 of them knew me, and I knew almost all of them. So whoever was there must have been at least half of them must have been my acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: In doing your medical job, you were in charge practically for the entire territory of Samac municipality. Did you, and how often, go to the villages that belong to municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: About six months before the war started, let's call it a war, I took part in an experimental project of house visits that our medical centre was doing together with the medical school in Tuzla, so we had a very nice project and we started working on it and implementing it. However, the project failed, most probably to technical difficulties, to put it that way, because at the time we visited the whole territory of municipality in a small car and we reached all places. However, since the times had already become rather strange, people had put guards everywhere, although I knew all those guards, and we passed through these checkpoints without any problems, but it was rather embarrassing. So eventually the project was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the motives for those guards and sentries to be posted in villages?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, probably they felt they need to protect themselves from anyone. I didn't [as interpreted] believe that Croatian villages had Croat guards, Serbian villages had Serb guards. We didn't have in Samac Muslim villages, but if we had had them, they would have had their guards. But as I said, we passed through these checkpoints and by these guards in a correct way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one small intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript. Here it is, page 90. The witness didn't say "I didn't believe that Croatian villages had Croat guards." It makes not much sense. He spoke that Croatian villages had Croat guards, Serbian villages Serbian guards. Just that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that can be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify, Doctor, this transcript. Could you please just speak a little bit more slowly, because the interpreters are having a problem keeping the pace. I asked you if you had any personal knowledge what the motives were and the reasons for posting village guards at the time, and for certain tensions to arise along ethnic lines, and you started to explain that -- maybe you can repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: All village guard posts that I passed through wore identical uniforms. Those were the uniforms of the war police, which means blue uniforms, just like the ones worn by the army. I remember that when I did my military service in the air force. I know that Serbs were manning those guard posts in Serbian villages, because I knew them personally. Equally, I know that Croats had their guards in Croatian villages, because I knew them personally as well. I thought that they were either doing some exercise or drill or were just exercising how to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February or March 1992, you were travelling from Samac to Brcko. Can you tell us something about what happened that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to travel, and Samac was under the blockade. Nobody was able to either go out or enter the town, since the chief of the police was a neighbour of mine, he -- we lived in the same building and the same entrance to the apartment building. I called him and asked him what was going on, and he told me that the town was under the blockade by members of the SDA and that I should wait, and as soon as he settles the matter, he will let me know and tell me that I can leave the town. He soon resolved -- the matter was soon resolved. He gave me a call and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This neighbour of yours who was the chief of the police, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Vinko. Vinko Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor: At your work in early 1992 until April, where did you work in Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992 until the war broke out, I worked in the department for occupational medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, because I presumed the staff of mixed ethnic origin, there were Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, how would you assess the atmosphere that prevailed among the co-workers there -- then, from the beginning of 1992, until April?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, the situation that was embroiling and brewing for some time could not be felt in the medical sense, because those were people with higher moral standards or responsibility, and we did not exactly get involved in these problems. Probably over coffee we had a tete-a-tete discussions, but officially there was no mention of that in the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Just before the war broke out in mid-April 1992, let's say, a couple of weeks or a month before that, did you notice anything unusual at work? Did everybody continue to come normally to work or were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The only thing that I found very odd was an enormous inflow of medicines and medical supplies. We received assistance from outside in medication, and we received aid in the form of gauzes, bandages, and other medical supplies that normally exist in hospitals. We even received an ambulance, which for a rather poor town like ours was really a major gift. Some of our colleagues went on holiday or on a sick leave. I even helped one of my colleagues to get through to Western Europe. I gave him a false order for his mother that she was purportedly ill. Fortunately, the lady wasn't sick at all. I was not interested what was underlying the reasons for their departure. The one I spoke about was a colleague of mine, and I believe that one should always offer help in hand to one's colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a ten-minute break. We shall resume our proceedings at 1625 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Stanimirovic, if you're not feeling well or if you're feeling too hot or anything, you have the right to inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I feel well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we were talking about the atmosphere in the medical centre. Could you please tell me who at that time, in the period from January 1992 until the beginning of the war or the conflict in Samac in April 1992, who was heading the medical institution where you worked? Who was the director?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The director was Dr. Anto Majic. He was a pediatrician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Anto is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After him, who was heading the medical centre from April 1992 until -- and onwards?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: After him, the coordinator, as it was called then, was Dr. Mesud Nogic. He was a gynaecologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... pausing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your instructions, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me until when was Dr. Nogic at the head of the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nogic was managing the medical centre until I returned from the Donja Slatina local clinic, where I was -- from where I was brought back to Samac, and this was sometime in September or October 1992. So then I substituted for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he leave Samac at that time or did he stay? And if he did, what was the post that he continued to work at?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nogic remained in Samac, and he worked in the gynaecology department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the ethnic composition was of the institution where you worked from January 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We heard -- only one small correction here on page 96. The witness said he was chief of gynaecology department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Where abouts?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Line 8. Line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Instead of just him remaining in the -- working in the gynaecology department, he was chief? Mr. Pantelic can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a correction for the transcript. What you said after you were appointed -- allow me to finish, please, sir, Dr. Stanimirovic. Could you please make a break also because of the transcript. So your answer to the question was that he, after you were appointed, remained and continued to work. Could you tell us what was his post and at which department in the medical centre did he work?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nogic remained at work in the medical centre as a gynaecologist. Since this is a specific service which other doctors cannot perform, they don't know how to perform it, and he was the only gynaecologist, naturally he was the head of the department. He was that also before the war. He is otherwise a person that I have full confidence in, and he's a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your personal knowledge is about the ethnic composition of the institution where you worked, roughly? You don't have to go into details. Was it a single ethnic group that comprised the staff, or was it multi-ethnic? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The composition of the employees at the medical centre was multi-ethnic: Croats, Serbs, and Muslims were employed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the composition, was it such from April 1992 until the end of 1993, or was it different?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: When the war began, I was at the Samac medical centre. Quite a few of us stayed behind. So the composition was varied. There were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. I was there at that place for a few days performing that duty. Then I was entrusted with the job of the sector clinic in Donja Slatina. That's where I was sent to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were appointed as the chief of the medical centre in the fall of 1992, what was the ethnic composition of your colleagues then?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Samac, to the medical centre, the staff was still multi-ethnic. There were fewer Muslims and Croats, but there were Muslims and Croats still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about any of your colleagues in the fall of 1992 who were no longer in the institution? Did you know where they went and why did they go?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: When I returned, naturally, the first thing was to see where my colleagues were, and then I heard from other colleagues that they had pulled out of Samac, they had left Samac, which I considered to be normal in given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as your Serb colleagues are concerned, did you notice any changes there in the personnel structure? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They all went to different posts, because -- to different places, because Samac is a place that was frequently shelled. So it was a little more difficult at that time to work in Samac. People were afraid. So they found ways to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
