utterances.text: When you mentioned how you remarked that a larger quantity of medical supplies appeared in the medical centre, what conclusion did you make? Did you have any information where this came from, and why?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This happened several months before the outbreak of the war, and all the doctors participated in the transport of the material, for example, when a vehicle arrived with the supplies, we would help the nurses and the other staff to carry that into the medical centre building. The director explained to us that we had to sort all of that out, gauze and bandages on one side and medicines on another side, and then the medicines were sorted according to groups, what each medicine was for. So this is what we did. We expected that something ugly would happen, most probably because we were already sinking into poverty. So we thought that the world was helping us and that this would always be something useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information about events in the period before the outbreak of the conflict? So I'm talking about the month of March, in the inner area of Samac, Odzak, Brod. Were there any events there which stick to your mind?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At that time you could cross the bridge over into Croatia, and we crossed there, to buy petrol. Of course, we had our personal ID. There was a checkpoint on the bridge, on one side and the other side. I crossed the bridge several times. I didn't have any problems, again because I know those people. But, you know, it was difficult for me to see a guard on each corner and to be watched while you were passing by, but that was the reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation in Croatia in the sense of armed conflict? Did that stop at that time or were they still going on? I'm talking about the first initial period from January 1992 until April 1992. That's the period I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't really tell you anything about that. I don't know. I wasn't really following that. It's something that I'm not really interested in. I didn't want to watch daily news or news on television. It was very sad. But sometimes you could hear cannon fire from a distance, and there was some information, so I was able to assume that fierce fighting was going on somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid-April, to be more specific, on the day between the 16th and the 17th of April, what do you remember about that specific period?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was at home that night. I was woken by firing. The first thought was that it was some kind of a holiday and that people who were celebrating that holiday had gotten drunk and that they were firing from their weapons, because that's a custom of ours. However, the shooting continued for a while, so I assumed that it was a major holiday. But then they told me that it wasn't a holiday at all [as interpreted]. So I thought that was a little strange. In the morning I went to work. At the time, I was working in a glass factory. It was producing glass for vehicles. When I got there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, Dr. Stanimirovic. Just one correction. What did you say, that you worked in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is another correction in the transcript. It is on page 101. He said they told me that it wasn't a holiday at all. He was speaking about his conversation with his wife. So this is not an accurate reproduction of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have it corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will -- yes, Your Honour. I will try to correct that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Stanimirovic, this part of the transcript, could you please repeat the following: You were asking yourself, was it a holiday. Who were you talking to?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I asked my wife, who was sleeping next to me at the time, since she is more religious than I am, she knows such things better than I do, and she told me that it wasn't any kind of church holiday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second thing which I would like to clarify here, I think that I heard you say that in the morning, on the 17th of April, you went to your job, and you mentioned something. What was it? Could you please repeat what it was?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the factory where there was a clinic serving the employees of the factory, I didn't find anybody there except the person at the entrance. The gatekeeper. And he didn't even stop me, because he knows me. Again, I came back to the entrance gate, to the main entrance, and I asked him, "What is going on? How come there's nobody here?" And he looked at me so strangely and said, "Doctor, what's the matter with you? There's shooting in town."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: In that period, in April 1992, where were you residing? Can you tell us where you were living in town?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived between the medical centre and the hospital, so that when I was going to the work, to work at the factory, I wouldn't go through the centre of the town, but I would go via another round about way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the factory?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was either at the entrance or the exit to Samac, depending on how you look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which side was it?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Towards Tisina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that east of Samac?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was upstream from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you notice on the way from your flat to your -- to the factory? What did you notice on the road and on the streets? How would you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is a transit road. It was empty. But when I'm driving, I listen to music usually, so that I wasn't really paying much attention to the fact that there wasn't that much traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any patrols or checkpoints or barricades on that road?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. This is a secondary, round about road, so there were no patrols or barricades on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you went to the clinic at Uniglas, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They called me from the medical centre to come back immediately, and I returned to the medical centre, and that's where I found a lot of my colleagues, amongst them my colleague Vuckovic, who told me, "Come and see what happened to me." And I did have something to see indeed, in one room in the medical centre. His father was lying there. He was dead. I asked him what happened, and he told me that he was killed. At that moment, I became very serious and I realised -- I understood some things which are very difficult to describe but which happened to me. War in my town, in Samac, looked like something quite impossible, and it seemed to be quite impossible. And that dead man showed me that in fact it was possible and that it was happening here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out any details about the circumstances of the death of your colleague's father?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he did not stop when stopped by a police officer, that he sped through -- when he was not allowed to pass, and that they opened fire, and that is how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us in that first period, those first few days, whether there were armed clashes, was there any shelling? Could you please describe those first few days for us, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Those first few days that I spent in Samac there was firing all over town. There were also powerful explosions. I am not able to say why these explosions happened. I don't know what they were, were they mortars, artillery shots, or whatever. But you could hear them. And so we immediately all together went to a cellar or basement underneath the lab, and we made a shelter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where the mortar shells were coming from and the other fire?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody dared to go outside to look, especially because we didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Samac? You said you spent a couple of days in Samac and that after that you went to a new job. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That was the sector clinic in Donja Slatina. It's a village near Samac. I think it's about seven kilometres away, and it's on the Samac-Brcko road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: Why did you go there, and how long did you stay there? What were you doing there? What were your duties, your activities while there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the basis was for my going there, but I was transferred there. My activities were to be -- to make a 24-hour clinic there, an emergency clinic there, which was supposed to work for 24 hours a day. I got one nurse, a male nurse, and one car. I went there. I organised the service as best as I could. And I stayed there until September or October. It's probably mid- or late September more rather than October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: While you were working in this clinic in Donja Slatina, what medical services did you render, in fact, to this clinic? Who were your patients? Can you describe this in a couple of sentences, how you were professionally engaged there?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was a clinic of the medical centre which became a clinic where everybody who was either dead or alive was brought to this clinic within the range of five or six or seven kilometres. Most of them were wounded and injured people and dead people, so people who were killed, and we occasionally had a sick patient. It is very interesting that in the war, because that already looked like a war, people very seldom get sick. So my chief duty and that of my staff was reduced to treating 50 or 53 dead people, around 200 severely injured people, and those lightly injured, we didn't even count.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the number of the dead and the wounded for the entire period that you spent in the Donja Slatina clinic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are conditional numbers. I cannot be accurate, because this is just my estimate. Because many of those people I didn't have time to put on record. I simply didn't have time for that. And this refers only to the period that I worked at this clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Could you please explain whether the reason or the cause of the wounds and the deaths of these people that you mentioned were combat operations, war, or can you explain where the front line was in respect to your clinic, and what happened with some more severe cases that you were not able to treat in your clinic?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The front line was on the one side about two kilometres away, and on the other side of the clinic it was 1.5 kilometres away. The clinic was situated on an asphalt road, or by the asphalt road. Mainly, the wounds or the deaths were caused by firearms or by shrapnels. When I say "shrapnels," I'm referring to grenades, to fragmentation mines, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with more severe cases that you were unable to treat in your clinic in Donja Slatina?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: All severe cases that arrived, we tried to make them able to survive the transportation to the village of Pelagicevo, where there was a military field hospital, and they had helicopters, and then they transported them further on. My duty was to make all the casualties, whether they were wounded or injured, et cetera, to make it to this hospital, to make sure that they make it to this hospital. This clinic was in a garage. It was not equipped properly. But nevertheless, we managed, and I think that during the transportation we lost only two lives, that all the others survived and made it to the hospital. However, I don't know what happened with those people after that. I knew about some of them who had returned, but most of all I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What ethnicity -- your patients were of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OZREN STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Donja Slatina? They were mainly Serbs. Mainly Serbs. But there were Croats as well, because the surrounding villages were Croatian villages. And there were Muslims. I know one particular case of a Muslim woman who was wounded by a shrapnel, and since our clinic was the nearest one, she came to us for help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Because I thought that we would work around 15 minutes more due to the technical problems that we suffered with the computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's not possible because of other commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As we have other cases to deal with. Yes. We will continue on Monday, Dr. Stanimirovic, at 1415 hours. So you come back to Court. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
